name: Shu'ayb (Jethro)
source: Stories of the Prophets — compiled from the Qur'an and authentic hadith
paras: Shu'ayb was sent to the people of Madyan, the merchant town on the caravan routes near the Gulf of Aqaba. He is often identified with Jethro, the father-in-law of Musa, and the scholars described him as the most eloquent of the prophets in speech.

His people had two sicknesses: the corruption of trade — cheating with weights and measures, debasing the scale, withholding what was owed — and the corruption of worship, serving invented deities beside Allah.

He called them to the pure centre: "O my people, worship Allah; you have no deity other than Him. There has come to you clear evidence from your Lord. So fulfil the measure and weight and do not deprive people of their due, and do not cause corruption on the earth after its reform." (Al-A'raf 7:85).

Shu'ayb taught that honesty in the market-place is part of tauhid itself: "That which is left by Allah for you is best for you, if you are believers." (Hud 11:86) — profit is not in fraud, but in what Allah leaves for you lawfully.

The chiefs of Madyan answered with threats: "O Shu'ayb, we do not understand much of what you say, and indeed we consider you among us as weak. Were it not for your family, we would have stoned you." (Hud 11:91). They even mocked his prayer: "Does your prayer command you that we should leave what our fathers worshipped...?" (Hud 11:87).

Shu'ayb's answer became a creed for every caller to Allah: "I only desire reform so far as I am able. And my success is not except through Allah. Upon Him I have relied, and to Him I return." (Hud 11:88).

They plotted to expel him and the believers from Madyan — and the punishment seized them: "So the earthquake seized them, and they became within their home [corpses] fallen prone." (Al-A'raf 7:91). The traders who cheated the scale could not stand before the Lord of the scale.

"Those who denied Shu'ayb — it was as though they had never resided there. Those who denied Shu'ayb were the losers." (Al-A'raf 7:92). And the Qur'an recalls the same nation again in the story of the Companions of the Forest (Ashab al-Aykah), burnt by the punishment of the Day of Shade.

Shu'ayb's mission joins worship to commerce: prayer that never reaches the marketplace is not the prayer he preached. Fair scales, honest contracts, and contentment with lawful profit are the fruit of tauhid.
